title: Fidan Courts Abu Dhabi as Lavrov Opens Door to S-400 Transfer; Ankara's Nuclear Debate Resurfaces
subhead: Turkey's foreign minister met UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed in Abu Dhabi while Russia signaled it may let Ankara offload its S-400s to a friendly third country. Together the two developments point to Ankara trying to convert its defense dilemmas into diplomatic currency.

sections.heading: Fidan in Abu Dhabi: Wooing the Gulf's Swing Player
sections.body:
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan met UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan in Abu Dhabi on Monday, according to the Emirati state news agency WAM and Iran International. The readout described the talks as covering bilateral ties and regional peace efforts, with the meeting taking place against the backdrop of the ongoing US-Iran war and the paralysed Strait of Hormuz.

The UAE has quietly emerged as one of the most consequential swing states in the current Gulf crisis: it has kept channels open to Tehran, hosts a large US military footprint, and is itself a candidate buyer of the S-400 systems Turkey wants to shed. That overlap gives the Fidan visit more substance than a routine diplomatic call.
sections.whyItMatters: Ankara is working the Gulf for both investment and diplomatic cover while the Hormuz closure reshapes regional alignments. The UAE's interest in the S-400s and its independent line toward Iran make it the natural broker Ankara needs.

sections.heading: Lavrov Signals Russia May Allow Turkey to Offload Its S-400s
sections.body:
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Moscow was willing to consider letting Turkey transfer its S-400 air defense systems to a third country, provided the recipient maintains friendly relations with Russia and guarantees the systems will never reach Ukraine. Speaking on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, Lavrov named no country but confirmed the UAE is among those reportedly interested, adding that no formal request had yet arrived — according to reporting by Hürriyet and relayed by the Kyiv Post.

The statement matters because the S-400s are the central obstacle to Turkey's return to the F-35 program. Under current US sanctions rules, Ankara must divest the Russian systems before the six F-35s it paid for in 2019 can be delivered. Semafor reported in August that the deal was 'at a standstill' for precisely this reason, and Senator Rick Scott has said flatly that Turkey 'cannot have the F-35' while it holds the S-400.

A parallel complication remains Israeli objections, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu arguing F-35 deliveries to Turkey would 'destroy the power balance in the Middle East' — concerns Semafor noted could also apply to a UAE transfer.
sections.whyItMatters: Russia has previously treated the S-400 end-user certificate as binding and refused to take the systems back, so this is a genuine softening. If a UAE transfer becomes viable, it removes the single biggest legal obstacle between Ankara and the F-35 — though Israeli and congressional resistance would still have to be cleared.

sections.heading: The Nuclear Question Returns to the Fore
sections.body:
A Cyprus Mail analysis published Monday traced Turkey's nuclear history and argued the Iran war has revived a question Ankara has never fully closed: whether it should seek a deterrent of its own. It cites Erdoğan's 2019 complaint that some states hold nuclear-armed missiles while Turkey is denied them — 'this I cannot accept' — and Fidan's February 2026 warning that if Iran acquired nuclear weapons, Turkey might 'inevitably' have to join the same race.

The piece notes concrete markers: Ankara is building Akkuyu, its first nuclear plant, though it is Russian-built, Russian-owned, and leaves Turkey dependent on Rosatom for fuel and technology. Turkey is also developing increasingly ambitious long-range missiles, and in 2025 its navy announced NUKDEN, a programme to master nuclear-powered submarine technology. Turkey remains an NPT member with IAEA safeguards and, for now, no industrial enrichment or reprocessing capability.
sections.whyItMatters: This is a debate piece, not a policy shift — but the framing is deliberate. Turkey is accumulating nuclear latency: reactors, missiles, submarine propulsion. The Iran war has supplied a live argument for why that latency might matter, and Ankara's partners are watching.

sections.heading: Fund Crisis: Ankara Lifts Freezes but Keeps the Squeeze On
sections.body:
Turkish prosecutors lifted asset restrictions on 45 companies and 19 investment funds caught up in the widening fund investigation, while police detained eight more people on Monday, per Turkish Minute and Reuters. The relief is narrow: a separate order to liquidate 131 funds holding assets belonging to 455,758 investors — worth roughly $18 billion — remains in force, and restrictions on individuals continue.

The Capital Markets Board clarified that all orders placed on the TEFAS fund-trading platform on September 17 had been cancelled and that investors would be paid from remaining assets proportionally, with no guarantee of full recovery. It had already extended the liquidation timetable from three to six months.

The scandal has now drawn political blood. Former family minister Fatma Betül Sayan Kaya resigned from her AKP leadership posts after opposition allegations that she and her husband traded Özata Denizcilik shares before the crash — a resignation Erdoğan accepted. Prosecutors have requested investor-level records from the Central Securities Depository to determine who sold before trading halted, following a New Party lawmaker's claim that some investors got advance warning.
sections.whyItMatters: Ankara is trying to show the system is functioning — freeing the clean, pursuing the guilty — without conceding that the liquidation itself is the loss. But the tip-off investigation targets the question that politically hurts most: who knew, and who got out first.

sections.heading: Aegean Rhetoric Flares Over a Hypothetical Greek Strike
sections.body:
Turkish media seized on Greek reporting about a hypothetical 'preemptive strike' against Turkey, with outlets including Hürriyet, Yeni Şafak and CNN Türk presenting it as evidence that Athens intends to hit first, according to Greek City Times. The story traces back to December 2025 remarks by General Dimitrios Houpis, chief of the Hellenic National Defence General Staff, about Greece needing the ability to deliver 'preemptive strategic strikes at great depth.'

Greek sources and Ta Nea framed this as deterrence doctrine rather than an attack plan — the scenario envisions a crisis over maritime zones escalating, with Greece deciding whether to act before a Turkish landing force left port. Both countries remain NATO members, and the underlying disputes over islands, continental shelf, EEZ and energy cables are unresolved.
sections.whyItMatters: Nothing new happened militarily — this is a rhetorical exchange recycled through both countries' media. But it shows how thin the margin is in the Aegean: a general's deterrence language becomes a war plan in the other capital, and each side's exercises feed the other's threat perception.

sections.heading: Kurdish File: Quiet Progress, Regional Pressure
sections.body:
In Turkey, the DEM Party elected Yunus Muratakan as co-chair of its Diyarbakır branch on Sunday, per Rudaw — a figure who, as a boy in 1996, spoke out publicly for Kurdish rights. The move signals continued party-level consolidation as the disarmament process grinds through its implementation phase.

Across the border, the Washington Kurdish Institute's September digest documented a sustained crackdown in Iranian Kurdistan (Rojhelat), centred on the September 16 general strike marking four years since Zhina Amini's death. Arrests touched shopkeepers, journalists, cultural figures and children, while lethal shootings along the Kurdish border continued. The digest recorded little publicly announced armed activity inside Rojhelat during the month.
sections.whyItMatters: Turkey's own Kurdish process is moving slowly and mostly out of the headlines, while the same Kurdish question stays highly combustible in Iran. Ankara has an obvious interest in a stable, quiet border — and a clear stake in monitoring whatever comes out of Rojhelat next.

bottomLine: No single drama today, but two threads worth watching came into focus. Russia's willingness to let Turkey sell its S-400s to a third country is the first real movement in years on the issue that blocks the F-35 deal — with the UAE, which Fidan just visited, as the likely end point. Meanwhile the fund crisis entered its accountability phase: asset freezes lifted, eight more detentions, and a former minister gone. Ankara is trying to demonstrate that its institutions work while protecting the political flanks, and the investigation into who traded on advance warning is the part that will decide whether the scandal stays an economic story or becomes a governing-party one.
sources: Turkish Minute, Reuters, Iran International, WAM/UAE state news, Kyiv Post, Hürriyet, Semafor, Chatham House, Cyprus Mail, Greek City Times, Ta Nea, Rudaw, Washington Kurdish Institute (dckurd.org), Anadolu Agency
